newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine clamps down again on corrupt bureaucrats.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine clamps down again on corrupt bureaucrats.

text.p: Ukraine, criticised abroad as a hotbed of corruption and under pressure to clear its name, vowed on Thursday to wrest temptation away from grasping bureaucrats.

"This campaign is about cleaning hands that are sticky from dirty money, money that has also been dirtying the hands of government officials," Justice Minister Serhiy Holovaty said in outlining President Leonid Kuchma's latest plans to fight corruption to a news conference.
"This is an important move by the president to take steps to remove this stain from our society," he added.

Ukraine, which has attracted only $1.4 billion in foreign investment since independence in 1991, has recently been accused in Western media reports of scaring off investors with widespread corruption and threats of violence.

"I'm certain these reports are tied...to the nervousness of Western nations, financial groups, investors and government officials at the state of our economy and at functionaries standing in the way of Ukraine's economic development," he said.

Although corruption and organised crime are prevalent in many former Soviet republics such as Russia, whose President Boris Yeltsin is due to visit Ukraine in June, Holovaty is one of few ministers to point the finger at government officials.

Kuchma first declared war on corruption after taking power in 1994, and this month he created a new investment commission partly aimed at reducing corruption in the cash-strapped former Soviet republic of 52 million people.
The 26-point programme lists preventive steps ordering government workers to submit a declaration of their activities, clearing the way for suspect officials to be sacked.

It also removes myriad licensing and permitting requirements which provide opportunities for government officials to demand numerous bribes from investors. "A corrupt functionary is chiefly interested in his own pocket, and is agreeable to doing anything possible and ensuring that whatever document or decision is approved, it will let him fill his pockets," Holovaty said.
The new programme also abolishes a law obliging businesses to have their books inspected quarterly by tax officials in order to reduce their their chances of demanding bribes.

Holovaty said about half a dozen ministries had asked to be exempt from the new ruling, and accused the Finance Ministry of actively blocking it. "It will work if everybody puts their energy behind it," he said.
